caption: The landscape around the Very Large Telescope, Cerro Paranal
story: Small silver shapes sit on a distant mountaintop, far across a bare landscape that looks almost like an alien world. They are the telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) on Cerro Paranal in Chile. ESO gave the photograph the title "The road to Paranal".

The shapes belong to two kinds of instrument. The larger ones are the VLT's Unit Telescopes, and the smaller ones are its Auxiliary Telescopes. From this distance they shrink to specks, which gives a feel for how much empty ground surrounds the observatory.

The photographer, Y. Beletsky, took the picture from a neighbouring peak. That mountain is an observing site in its own right, home to another ESO facility, the Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy, known as VISTA. The two summits are close enough that one observatory can be photographed from the other.

understand.summary: A landscape photograph credited to ESO and Y. Beletsky. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: No camera details are published, so it is unclear how closely the photograph matches what an eye would see from the same spot.

alt: Tiny silver shapes, the telescopes of the Very Large Telescope, on the distant mountain of Cerro Paranal.

caption: An Auxiliary Telescope under a multicoloured sky, Paranal Observatory
story: A telescope in the foreground is lit by a yellow-green glow, while the sky above ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile runs through blues, purples, oranges, greens, yellows and reds. The telescope is one of the Auxiliary Telescopes of the Very Large Telescope (VLT).

The VLT has four of these auxiliaries, each 1.8 metres across, working alongside four much larger 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes. The Auxiliary Telescopes are self-contained and mobile. Depending on what an observing project needs, each one can be moved along a network of tracks to as many as 30 different observing positions.

When the telescopes work together as the VLT Interferometer, each gathers light from the same target and sends it through mirrors in underground tunnels to a shared focal point. Combining light in this way lets astronomers pick out much finer detail than a single telescope could manage.
explore: ESO calls the eight-telescope VLT the world's most advanced visible-light observatory. Its resolution is sharp enough to reveal detail on the surface of a star and to examine the region around a black hole. ESO titled the picture "When Light Collides".

understand.summary: A night landscape photograph of the observatory credited to ESO and Y. Beletsky. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: Long camera exposures usually gather more light than the eye can, so the colours may not look the same to someone standing at the site.

alt: A Very Large Telescope Auxiliary Telescope bathed in a yellow-green glow beneath a sky of blues, purples, oranges, greens, yellows and reds.

caption: The Great Rift and zodiacal light above Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory
story: Dark clouds run vertically through the frame and appear to cut the Milky Way's river of starlight in half above NSF NOIRLab's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO). These clouds are the Great Rift, a vast complex of dust between the stars.

The rift shows that our galaxy holds far more than stars. It also contains enormous amounts of interstellar dust, and the Great Rift alone holds about a million Suns' worth. The grains are ultrafine, roughly ten times smaller than pollen, but together they hide the light of the brightest part of the Milky Way.

A second band of dust crosses the picture, sloping down from the top left. This white glow is zodiacal light, sunlight reflected by interplanetary dust inside our Solar System. The Great Rift is dark and lies far beyond our neighbourhood, while this dust is close and bright. In the upper left of the glow, three planets form a triangle. From left to right they are Venus, Mars and Saturn.
explore: The photograph was made during the NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition, which visited all of NOIRLab's sites. The photographer, Tomas Slovinský, is a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador. NOIRLab released the picture as one of its Image of the Week features.

understand.summary: A night-sky landscape photograph by Tomas Slovinský. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the Milky Way and the zodiacal light would look fainter to someone standing at the site.

alt: The Milky Way split vertically by dark dust clouds above an observatory, with a diagonal band of white zodiacal light at upper left containing three planets.

caption: The McMath-Pierce Solar Telescope, Kitt Peak National Observatory
story: The decommissioned McMath-Pierce Solar Telescope sits at the centre of this photograph from NSF NOIRLab's Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO). It saw first light in 1962, kept working for 55 years and was retired in 2017. For much of that time it was the largest solar telescope on Earth.

Solar astronomy turns the usual problem around. Most telescopes struggle to collect enough light from faint, distant targets. The Sun is close by astronomical standards and by far the brightest object in the Solar System, so light is plentiful. What comes with it is heat. Sunlight warms the air inside a solar telescope's tunnel, and that warm air distorts the data.

The designers fought the heat with special paint, pipes carrying a cooling liquid, and the natural chill of the ground below. Together these kept the bottom of the 61-metre (200-foot) optical path about 6 °C (11 °F) cooler than the outside air.
explore: Although it no longer observes the Sun, the building has a new purpose. When the photograph was released, NOIRLab was converting it into an outreach facility, NOIRLab's Windows on the Universe Center for Astronomy Outreach. The credit names the photographer as B. Tafreshi.

understand.summary: A photograph of the telescope at Kitt Peak credited to B. Tafreshi. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: No exposure details are published, so it is unclear how closely the photograph matches what an eye would see.

alt: The McMath-Pierce Solar Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory.

caption: Sunset colours over Kitt Peak National Observatory
story: The Arizona sky glows with vivid colour as the Sun goes down over NSF NOIRLab's Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO). The colours come from sunlight scattering on its way through Earth's atmosphere.

KPNO stands in the Arizona-Sonoran Desert, and dry places like this tend to show clearer sunset colours than regions where rain and humid weather arrive almost every day. Heavier particles in the air, such as water vapour, absorb some of the sunlight and wash the colours out. In dry desert air the light reaches our eyes largely unobstructed. Arizona's sparse population helps as well, keeping the air clean and pollution low.

The conditions that sharpen a sunset also help astronomers once it is dark. The hot, cleaner air lets them record sharper data of the visible sky after nightfall, which is part of what makes the site useful for research.
explore: The photograph was taken during the NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition, which visited all of NOIRLab's sites. The credit names the photographer as T. Slovinský. It appeared as one of NOIRLab's Image of the Week releases.

understand.summary: A landscape photograph of the sunset sky at Kitt Peak. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: Sunset colours are visible to the naked eye, though camera settings can change how strong they look in a photograph.

alt: The sky over Kitt Peak National Observatory glowing in vivid sunset colours.

caption: Telescopes under the Milky Way, Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory
story: The Milky Way fills the sky behind a group of telescopes at NSF NOIRLab's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO). The Thai Southern Hemisphere Telescope stands in the foreground, and five of the seven PROMPT telescopes are clustered behind it. With our home galaxy as a backdrop, the telescopes are easy to overlook.

The Thai telescope is part of the Thai Robotic Telescope Network (TRTN), run by the National Astronomical Research Institute of Thailand (NARIT). As its name suggests, the telescope is the network's instrument in the southern hemisphere.

PROMPT stands for Panchromatic Robotic Optical Monitoring and Polarimetry Telescopes. Robotic telescopes can carry out observations without an astronomer at the controls. Panchromatic means working across a wide range of colours, and polarimetry is the measurement of how light waves are oriented, which can reveal details that brightness alone does not.
explore: The credit names B. Tafreshi as the photographer. The Milky Way is our home galaxy, and from a dark site its crowded disc appears as a long band of light across the sky.

understand.summary: A night landscape photograph by B. Tafreshi. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the Milky Way would look fainter to someone standing among these telescopes.

alt: Several telescopes at Cerro Tololo, led by the Thai Southern Hemisphere Telescope in front, beneath the Milky Way.

caption: The WIYN 3.5-meter Telescope under the Milky Way, Kitt Peak National Observatory
story: The Milky Way rises from the horizon behind the Wisconsin-Indiana-Yale-NOIRLab (WIYN) 3.5-meter Telescope, which seems to be watching it. A reddish airglow, a natural phenomenon, tints the horizon. The telescope stands at NSF NOIRLab's Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO).

KPNO lies on the Tohono O'odham Nation, in the Arizona-Sonoran Desert. The clear view of part of our galaxy's plane shows why the site suits the study of faint objects. Light pollution is low, the air is dry, and the sky is darker than magnitude 20. Magnitude is the astronomers' scale of brightness, and higher numbers mean fainter light.

Those conditions have let researchers in the WIYN Consortium observe galaxies, nebulas, exoplanets and many other targets. They work with the 3.5-meter telescope and with its smaller sibling, the WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope.
explore: The credit names the photographer as R. Sparks. Airglow is faint light given off by Earth's upper atmosphere itself, which is why it can tint the sky even at a dark site.

understand.summary: A night landscape photograph by R. Sparks. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the Milky Way and airglow would look fainter in person.

alt: The WIYN telescope at Kitt Peak with the Milky Way spilling up from a reddish horizon.

caption: The cometary globule CG4, imaged by the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: This picture from the NSF Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope shows CG4, a cometary globule. Cometary globules are isolated clouds of gas and dust in our galaxy. They get their name because their shape can resemble a comet's head and tail, although they have nothing to do with comets.

The telescope's Mosaic II camera recorded CG4 through four filters. Three let through blue, green and near-infrared light. The fourth isolates one particular shade of red, called hydrogen-alpha, which warm hydrogen gas gives off.

Pairing broad filters with a narrow one is a common approach in astronomical imaging. The broad filters record the general colours of stars and dust, while the hydrogen-alpha filter shows where glowing hydrogen is found. The near-infrared filter reaches just beyond the red end of what the eye can see.
explore: The blue filter is centred at 438 nm, the green at 538 nm, the near-infrared at 820 nm and the hydrogen-alpha filter at 657 nm.

understand.summary: The Blanco 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic II camera observed CG4 through blue, green, near-infrared and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colours assigned to each filter in the final picture are not published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, so part of what the camera recorded could never be seen directly.

alt: The cometary globule CG4, imaged by the Blanco 4-meter Telescope.

caption: The SOAR Telescope under the Milky Way, Cerro Pachón
story: The Milky Way seems to pour out of an open dome and spill across a colourful sky. The dome houses the Southern Astrophysical Research (SOAR) Telescope on Cerro Pachón in Chile, operated by NSF NOIRLab's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO). Near the horizon, a wash of yellow and green comes from airglow mixed with light pollution from nearby villages. Where those two colours meet, at lower left, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds shine through.

Near the centre of the frame sits the constellation Crux, also called the Southern Cross. It can be found by its red star at the top of the cross and the three nearby blue stars that complete the shape.

European and Pacific Islander navigators have steered by this group of stars for centuries. It plays a part like Polaris in the north, but where Polaris guides travellers north, Crux points roughly towards the South Pole.
explore: The photograph is huge, at 900 megapixels, and was taken during the NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition to all of NOIRLab's sites. Its photographer, Tomas Slovinský, is a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador.

understand.summary: A night-sky landscape photograph by Tomas Slovinský. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the Milky Way and Magellanic Clouds would look fainter to someone at the site.

alt: The Milky Way rising from the open dome of the SOAR Telescope into a sky tinted yellow and green near the horizon, with the Magellanic Clouds at lower left.

caption: The Crab Nebula (Messier 1), imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: This portrait of Messier 1, the Crab Nebula, comes from the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope at NSF NOIRLab's Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO). The Crab is a supernova remnant, the spreading debris of a star that exploded.

Its history runs through modern astronomy. British astronomer John Bevis recorded it in 1731 and took it for a cloudy blob. More than three decades later the French comet hunter Charles Messier showed it was a real object, and it became the first entry in his catalogue of nebulae and star clusters. In the early 20th century, astronomers tied it to a supernova that Chinese astronomers had seen in 1054, making it the first object linked to a previously recorded supernova.

In 1968 astronomers found a pulsar inside the nebula at radio wavelengths. A pulsar is the ultra-dense, fast-spinning core left behind by the star. A year later John Cocke, Donald Taylor and Michael Disney confirmed it in visible light using KPNO's UArizona 0.9-meter Spacewatch Telescope.
explore: It was the Mayall telescope's final image before DESI, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, went in, and the Crab had also been its first target at first light in 1973. The Crab Pulsar was the first to connect a historical supernova with a pulsar of precisely known age.

understand.summary: The Mayall telescope's Mosaic-3 camera observed the nebula in visible light through filters for oxygen III, hydrogen-alpha and the i band. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The nebula is far too faint for the eye to see in this detail, and a long camera exposure gathers much more light than the eye can.

alt: The Crab Nebula, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope.

caption: The Taffy Galaxies UGC 12914 and UGC 12915, imaged by Gemini North
story: Two galaxies with a twisted look appear in this picture from the Gemini North telescope. They are UGC 12914 and UGC 12915, nicknamed the Taffy Galaxies, and they lie about 150 million light-years away. Gemini North is one of the two telescopes of the International Gemini Observatory, which NSF NOIRLab operates.

Their contorted shapes are the aftermath of a head-on collision. It happened about 25 million years before the moment recorded in the light we now receive from them. Because light takes time to cross space, the picture shows the pair as they were when that light set out.

Between the two galaxies stretches a bridge of highly turbulent gas, and the nickname calls to mind taffy pulled between two hands. For all the gas it holds, the bridge is devoid of significant star formation.
explore: NOIRLab's Communication, Education & Engagement team produced the picture for the NOIRLab Legacy Imaging Program. Gemini North's GMOS-N instrument recorded it through g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters.

understand.summary: Gemini North's GMOS-N instrument observed the galaxies in visible light through g, r and i filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter, which isolates red light from hydrogen gas. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Galaxies this distant are far too faint to see without a large telescope, and the camera builds up their light over long exposures.

alt: The Taffy Galaxies UGC 12914 and UGC 12915, two galaxies with a twisted appearance.

caption: Betelgeuse above the Bok 2.3-meter Telescope, Kitt Peak National Observatory
story: A single orange star stands out at the centre of a multicoloured night sky above the UArizona Bok 2.3-meter Telescope at NSF NOIRLab's Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO). Faraway city lights, passing cars, airglow and the Milky Way's arc all add to the mix of colours. On the right, zodiacal light rising from the horizon crosses the Milky Way.

The orange star is Betelgeuse, a red supergiant that marks a shoulder of Orion, the hunter. As a relatively old star it glows a cooler red than its hot blue neighbours, but it is usually still the 10th brightest star in the night sky. It is also enormous, more than 750 times the Sun's diameter, so no bigger star can be seen without a telescope.

In 2019 astronomers saw a small explosion on its surface, and the news fed speculation that a supernova was near. In 2021 scientists concluded that the dying star will not explode for at least another 100,000 years.
explore: The photograph was taken by T. Slovinský during the NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition, which visited all of NOIRLab's sites. NOIRLab released it as one of its Image of the Week features.

understand.summary: A night-sky landscape photograph by T. Slovinský. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the night sky would look fainter to someone standing at the site.

alt: An orange star at the centre of a multicoloured night sky above the Bok telescope at Kitt Peak, with the arc of the Milky Way.

caption: Star trails above Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Cerro Pachón
story: Circular star trails spin above Cerro Pachón in northern Chile, home of the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. The very long exposure records the apparent motion of the stars, along with other moving things such as aircraft and satellites, and the trails hint at the range of colours and brightnesses among the stars. At the centre of the circles lies the southern celestial pole, in the dim constellation Octans, the Octant.

Studying the properties of stars with observatories like Rubin helps scientists learn how stars evolve. Across the 10-year survey known as the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), Rubin is expected to measure about 17 billion stars.

When Rubin spots a star changing in brightness, it will issue an alert within minutes. Astronomers can then follow short- and long-term changes that are hard to track without a continuous survey. These include flickers or pulses ahead of supernovae, new variable stars whose brightness shifts over several years, and rare events such as mergers of dense neutron stars.
explore: Rubin is funded jointly by the U.S. National Science Foundation and the Office of Science within the U.S. Department of Energy, and run together by NSF NOIRLab and DOE's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. The photographer, Hernán Stockebrand, works at Rubin Observatory as a DevOps Engineer and is also a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador.

understand.summary: An extra-long-exposure night photograph by Hernán Stockebrand. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points, and the trails appear only because the camera kept recording while Earth turned.

alt: Circular star trails in many colours spinning above the Rubin Observatory on Cerro Pachón.

caption: The Big Dipper over Kitt Peak National Observatory
story: On the left stands the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope, and on the right the UA Bok 2.3-meter Telescope, both at NSF NOIRLab's Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO). High in the sky to the right, above the Mayall, are the stars of the Big Dipper, and a faint glow hangs over the Bok telescope. The mountain hosts twenty optical and two radio telescopes, one of the largest gatherings of astronomical instruments in the northern hemisphere.

The Big Dipper is an asterism, a recognisable pattern within the larger constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear. Its stars are circumpolar. They sit so close to the north celestial pole that at most northern latitudes they never set. They stay above the horizon in daytime too, hidden only by the far brighter sunlight.
The glow over the Bok telescope is the Gegenschein. It is sunlight reflected by interplanetary dust in the part of the sky opposite the Sun.
explore: The photograph was taken during the NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition, which visited all of NOIRLab's sites. The photographer, Tomáš Slovinský, is a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador. The picture appeared as a NOIRLab Image of the Week.

understand.summary: A night-sky landscape photograph by Tomáš Slovinský. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the faint Gegenschein would be much harder to see in person.

alt: Two telescopes at Kitt Peak under a night sky, with the Big Dipper high at right and a faint glow above the right-hand telescope.

caption: The galaxies NGC 4411 and NGC 4410, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: At the centre of this wide view sits NGC 4411, a calm-looking pair of spiral galaxies, with NGC 4411b on the left and NGC 4411a on the right. Above them is NGC 4410, a group of galaxies that are clearly interacting.

NGC 4411 plays a visual trick. The two spirals are thought to be neighbours, both about 50 million light-years from us, but they show no signs of interaction such as distorted arms. NGC 4411a is especially satisfying to look at, with distinct, symmetrical spiral arms that wind more than 360 degrees around its core.

NGC 4410 shows what a real interaction looks like. Its four galaxies are far more tangled and are joined by tidal bridges, streams of material drawn out as the gravity of each galaxy pulls on the others. If the two spirals of NGC 4411 were interacting, they would look similarly intertwined. Their neat, undisturbed shapes show no sign of that, even though the pair are thought to be close neighbours.
explore: The Dark Energy Camera (DECam), built by the Department of Energy, sits at the prime focus of the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at NSF NOIRLab's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile. It took this image for the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys, which picked targets for the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI).

understand.summary: DECam on the Blanco telescope observed the galaxies in visible and near-infrared light through g, r, i and z filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: These galaxies are far too faint to see without a telescope, and the z filter reaches into near-infrared light that the eye cannot see.

scaleExtra: Both galaxies of NGC 4411 are thought to lie about 50 million light-years from us, according to NOIRLab.
alt: Two calm spiral galaxies side by side at centre, with a tangled group of interacting galaxies above them.

caption: Lasers and star trails over Gemini North, Maunakea
story: Star trails blur across the sky and laser beams streak upward in this long exposure taken from Pu‘u Poli‘ahu, the peak next to the Gemini North telescope on Maunakea in Hawai‘i. Gemini North, which belongs to NSF NOIRLab's International Gemini Observatory, sits just right of centre firing its laser. A handful of other telescopes belonging to the Maunakea Observatories stand around it.

The beams may resemble searchlights or a science-fiction battle, but their job is to help the telescopes see clearly. They are part of adaptive optics systems, which measure how turbulence in the atmosphere distorts the incoming light.

Those measurements feed continuously into computer-controlled deformable mirrors that change shape to cancel the distortion. The correction removes almost all of the blurring caused by Earth's atmosphere, which gives Gemini North a view of the night sky that rivals a telescope in space, above the turbulent air.
explore: The credit names the photographer as J. Chu. The lasers help correct the vision of other cutting-edge telescopes as well as Gemini North.

understand.summary: A long-exposure night photograph by J. Chu. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as points, and the trails appear only because the camera kept recording as Earth turned.

alt: Laser beams shooting from telescopes on a mountaintop into a sky streaked with star trails.

caption: Moonrise over three telescopes, Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory
story: A huge-looking Moon rises over three telescopes at NSF NOIRLab's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO), high in the Andes of Chile, as another night of observing begins. From left to right they are the SMARTS–GSU 0.9-meter Telescope, the SMARTS–GSU 1.5-meter Telescope and the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope. The two SMARTS–GSU telescopes are run by the Georgia State University Research Foundation.
Some of the Moon's size comes from the camera lens. But people have noticed since ancient times that the Moon looks larger near the horizon. This Moon illusion is produced entirely by the brain.

A simple test proves it. Hold out your thumb when the Moon is high, and it is about the size of your thumbnail. Try again as it rises or sets, and it is still the size of your nail. There is no definitive explanation yet, but several factors play a part. When the Moon peeks out from behind mountains or buildings, those familiar shapes can lead the brain to judge it as closer.
explore: The photographer, Hernán Stockebrand, is a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador. NOIRLab also published a second photograph from the same spot, taken with the Moon higher above the horizon, so the two can be compared.

understand.summary: A night landscape photograph by Hernán Stockebrand. The camera lens enlarges the Moon to some degree. No other camera details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: The camera lens makes the Moon look bigger than the eye would see it, although the eye's own Moon illusion also makes it seem large near the horizon.

alt: A large Moon rising above three telescopes on a mountain at Cerro Tololo.

caption: The nebula M43, imaged from the Kitt Peak Visitor Center
story: A sphere of glowing pink hydrogen gas surrounds a very bright star in this picture of M43, part of the much larger Orion Nebula complex. The image was made at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center through its Advanced Observing Program (AOP).

The star is an extremely bright OB star. OB stars are hot, massive stars of the O and B types, and they pour out ultraviolet light. This one is carving out what astronomers call a matter-bounded Strömgren sphere. Its radiation ionizes the gas nearby, and the ionized hydrogen glows. How far the sphere reaches depends on the density of the gas and dust around the star.
IC 1274 is another good example of the same process. The clouds of gas in M43 are also raw material for the future, since many new stars will form from them.
explore: The photograph is credited to Pat and Chris Lee and Adam Block, working through the Advanced Observing Program at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center. It was taken during 2014.

understand.summary: The image was taken with a CCD camera at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center's roll-off-roof observatory, through blue, green, red and broadband filters. The glowing hydrogen appears pink, but the full colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Through an eyepiece the nebula would look fainter, because a camera builds up light over long exposures.

scaleExtra: M43 and the Orion Nebula lie around 1500 light-years away, according to NOIRLab.
alt: A bright star surrounded by a sphere of glowing pink hydrogen gas in the nebula M43.

caption: The Great Rift above Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Cerro Pachón
story: Above NSF NOIRLab's Vera C. Rubin Observatory on Cerro Pachón, the Great Rift seems to divide the Milky Way. The dark band is made of a chain of cold dust clouds where stars are actively forming. The clouds are so dense that they block the light of the stars behind them, and that blocking creates the rift.

The U.S. National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy fund Rubin jointly. At the time of this release it was due to start science operations in late 2025. Once complete, it was to use an 8.4-meter mirror and the largest astronomical camera ever built for a decade-long survey called the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), imaging the whole southern sky every 3–4 nights.

One planned goal was to catch transients, objects whose brightness or position changes quickly, such as supernovae, variable stars and asteroids. Transients can reveal processes that shape the Universe, and frequent observations like Rubin's are expected to push astronomy forward in ways no one can yet predict.
explore: Rubin is a Program of NSF NOIRLab, which was to operate it jointly with SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. The photograph was taken by Hernán Stockebrand, a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador, and appeared as a NOIRLab Image of the Week.

understand.summary: A night-sky landscape photograph by Hernán Stockebrand. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the night sky would look fainter to someone standing at the site.

alt: The Milky Way split by a dark band of dust clouds above the Rubin Observatory on Cerro Pachón.

caption: Sunset over Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Cerro Pachón
story: Golden sunlight slides across the rolling foothills of the Andes in this bird's-eye view of the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory on Cerro Pachón, in Chile's Coquimbo Region. NOIRLab describes the view from up there as like nowhere else on Earth.

The region's climate is the reason Rubin was built here. The selection weighed the number of clear nights each year, seasonal weather patterns and the stability of the local atmosphere, which astronomers call seeing. Good seeing lets a telescope separate fine details.

The choice paid off. When Rubin first turned to the sky during its First Look campaign in June 2025, the seeing proved excellent. The evidence is one of its first releases, a vast, finely detailed image of the Trifid and Lagoon Nebulae. On 30 June 2026 Rubin started its 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time.
explore: Rubin is funded jointly by the U.S. National Science Foundation and the Office of Science within the U.S. Department of Energy, and operated together by NSF NOIRLab and DOE's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. The picture also exists in a fulldome format. Its photographer, Theofanis Matsopoulos, is a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador.

understand.summary: A high-angle landscape photograph by Theofanis Matsopoulos. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: Sunset light is easy to see with the naked eye, though camera settings can change how the colours look in a photograph.

alt: A bird's-eye view of the Rubin Observatory on Cerro Pachón, with golden sunlight across the rolling Andean foothills.

caption: Star trails around the south celestial pole, Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: Stars swirl around the south celestial pole above the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in this timelapse image. Near the middle of the vortex sits Sigma Octantis, the southern hemisphere's pole star, which is fainter than Polaris, its better-known northern counterpart. Up and to the left of the telescope, the lit paths of two satellites cut across the star trails.

Photographers build timelapses like this by stacking many long-exposure images of the night sky. As Earth turns through the night, the stars appear to circle the celestial poles, the north one or the south one depending on the hemisphere.

The red squiggles in the foreground were made by someone walking with a red flashlight. Observatories commonly use red lights to protect night vision, because eyes that have adjusted to the dark are less sensitive to red light.
explore: The Blanco Telescope crowns Cerro Tololo, a summit in northern Chile that is home to NSF NOIRLab's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO). The credit names the photographer as D. Munizaga.

understand.summary: A timelapse made by combining long-exposure night photographs, credited to D. Munizaga. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points, and the trails appear only because the camera kept recording while Earth turned.

alt: Star trails circling the south celestial pole above the Blanco telescope, crossed by two satellite paths, with red light squiggles in the foreground.

caption: The Blanco 4-meter Telescope under green airglow and the Milky Way, Cerro Tololo
story: The Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at NSF NOIRLab's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile stands against the bright Milky Way. Above a layer of clouds, the sky glows green.

That green light is airglow. It appears when trace particles and gases in the atmosphere become electrically charged, or ionized. At night their atoms recombine and give off light of their own, producing a faint glow across the sky.

Airglow is so faint that people seldom see it with the naked eye. Long-exposure photographs like this one capture it more easily. It is one reason the night sky is never completely dark, even at sites far from light pollution. On its own, though, it does not usually cause serious trouble for astronomers observing at night.
explore: The credit names the photographer as B. Tafreshi. NOIRLab released the picture as one of its Image of the Week features, under the title "A Blanket of Light".

understand.summary: A long-exposure night photograph by B. Tafreshi. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: Airglow is rarely visible to the naked eye, and long-exposure photographs capture it much more easily.

alt: The Blanco telescope set against the bright Milky Way, with a green glow in the sky above a layer of clouds.

caption: Star trails around Polaris above Kitt Peak National Observatory
story: The scene looks like daytime, but star trails circle through the night sky in this long exposure of NSF NOIRLab's Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO). On the highest peak stands the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope. Almost directly above it, at the centre of the rings of star trails, sits Polaris, the North Star.

Polaris stays put because it lies at the north celestial pole, in line with the axis Earth spins around. As the planet turns, every other star seems to wheel around it, and a long exposure records those paths as arcs.

On the horizon, the lights of Tucson, Arizona, glow yellow about 89 kilometers (55 miles) to the northeast. NOIRLab's citizen science campaign Globe at Night invites stargazers of every age to help monitor light pollution in their own cities, wherever in the world they live.
explore: Light from nearby towns brightens the sky and makes faint objects harder to study, which is why a glow like Tucson's matters to observatories. Campaigns such as Globe at Night gather measurements of that glow from many places at once.

understand.summary: A long-exposure night photograph of Kitt Peak credited to KPNO/NOIRLab. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points, and the trails appear only because the camera kept recording while Earth turned.

alt: Concentric star trails circling Polaris above the Mayall telescope on Kitt Peak, with the yellow glow of Tucson on the horizon.

caption: Gemini North above a sea of clouds, Maunakea
story: At first glance Gemini North seems to stand on a seashore, with waves rolling below. The waves are in fact a rippling deck of cloud, and across it stretches the shadow of Maunakea, reaching for miles. The mountain's highest point, at far right, catches the light of the setting Sun while shadow falls over the telescope.

Gemini North is one of the two telescopes forming the International Gemini Observatory, run by NSF NOIRLab. Its site lies more than 4000 meters (13,000 feet) up, high above the clouds in the picture. As the day closes, its working hours begin.

The photograph makes one advantage of such a remote, high site easy to see. With the cloud deck spread out below, the sky above Gemini North is exceptionally clear and well suited to a night of astronomical observing.

understand.summary: A sunset landscape photograph by J. Chu. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: No camera details are published, so it is unclear how closely the photograph matches what an eye would see from the summit.

alt: The Gemini North telescope above a rippling deck of cloud, with the shadow of Maunakea stretching across it and the summit lit by the setting Sun at far right.

caption: Sunset over Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory
story: An unusually rich, colourful sunset fills the sky behind NSF NOIRLab's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO). A small clamshell dome sits in the foreground, and a tall metal frame topped by a canvas dome stands in the background at left.

Clouds can make for a fine sunset, but water vapour in the atmosphere also hampers astronomy by absorbing starlight. Astronomers and engineers have built a set of instruments to measure the effect. The clamshell dome houses one of them, aTmCam, the Atmospheric Transmission Monitoring Camera. It is a new calibration system that tells astronomers how much light is getting through the atmosphere.

The frame at left belongs to another atmospheric instrument at CTIO, the DIMM2 Seeing Monitor. It runs automatically and measures seeing, the degree to which turbulence in the air blurs astronomical observations.
explore: The credit names the photographer as B. Tafreshi. Between them, aTmCam and DIMM2 track two different ways the atmosphere affects observations: how much light gets through, and how much turbulence blurs it.

understand.summary: A sunset landscape photograph by B. Tafreshi. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: Sunset colours are visible to the naked eye, though camera settings can change how strong they look in a photograph.

alt: A colourful sunset sky over Cerro Tololo, with a small clamshell dome in the foreground and a tall metal frame with a canvas dome at left.

caption: Zodiacal light beside the Mayall 4-meter Telescope, Kitt Peak National Observatory
story: On the western horizon, below the glittering band of the Milky Way, a cone of hazy pastel light rises in this view of the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope at NSF NOIRLab's Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO). The cone is zodiacal light.

The glow follows the ecliptic, which is the plane of our Solar System and the Sun's path across the sky. That is why it shows up just before dawn breaks or just after dusk ends. Its soft white glow has earned it the nicknames false dawn and false dusk.

The resemblance is only on the surface. The reddish skies of a real dawn or dusk are produced by Earth's atmosphere, while zodiacal light begins far beyond our planet. It is sunlight reflected by interplanetary dust lying between the inner planets of the Solar System, so this glow comes from a much greater distance than any sunset colour.
explore: The credit names the photographer as P. Horálek of the Institute of Physics in Opava. NOIRLab released the picture as an Image of the Week under the title "A False Dawn at KPNO".

understand.summary: A night-sky landscape photograph by P. Horálek. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the night sky would look fainter to someone standing at the site.

alt: A cone of hazy pastel light rising from the western horizon beneath the glittering band of the Milky Way, with the Mayall telescope at Kitt Peak in view.

caption: Zodiacal light and airglow over the Blanco 4-meter Telescope, Cerro Tololo
story: A dim white gleam rises vertically on the left side of this photograph. On the right, beside the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at NSF NOIRLab's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO), bands of coloured light lie along the horizon. Two different effects light up this night sky.

The white gleam is zodiacal light, which is sunlight scattered by dust drifting between the planets of our Solar System. The light starts at the Sun and reaches us only after bouncing off those tiny grains.

The coloured bands are airglow, and they begin much closer to home, in Earth's own atmosphere. Gases high in the atmosphere give off a faint light of their own at night, and here that light tints the sky close to the horizon.
explore: The credit names the photographer as B. Tafreshi. NOIRLab released the photograph as an Image of the Week under the title "Sky Aglow at CTIO". Of the two glows it shows, only airglow comes from Earth itself.

understand.summary: A night-sky landscape photograph by B. Tafreshi. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: Both zodiacal light and airglow are faint, and a long camera exposure gathers far more of their light than the eye can.

alt: A dim white vertical glow on the left of a night sky and coloured bands along the horizon to the right of the Blanco telescope.

caption: Satellite streaks beside the Gemini North telescope
story: The broken streaks left of Gemini North are satellites crossing the sky, identified by the gaps in their trails. Gemini North is one of the two telescopes of the International Gemini Observatory, which NSF NOIRLab operates with partial support from the U.S. National Science Foundation.

The night sky is always moving, even if the naked eye cannot tell. A long exposure records that motion as trails left by stars, meteors and, more and more, satellites in orbit around Earth. Satellites have long been vital tools in fields such as hydrology and geology, but in recent years their numbers have soared for new uses such as broadband internet access.

Most satellite constellations cannot be seen with the unaided eye, especially where skies are already light-polluted. Sensitive camera detectors on telescopes like Gemini North pick up their reflected light easily, and that light affects astronomical data. NSF NOIRLab is working to reduce the impact of satellites on observations and to protect the sky near observatories from all light pollution.
explore: NSF NOIRLab co-hosts CPS, a centre for protecting dark and quiet skies, which was recently renewed for a 5-year extension. The photographer, Jeff Warner, documents how the sky is changing as satellite launches increase.

understand.summary: A long-exposure night photograph by Jeff Warner. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: Most satellite constellations are invisible to the unaided eye, and the camera's long exposure turns their passage into streaks.

alt: Broken streaks of satellite light crossing the sky to the left of the Gemini North telescope, among star trails.

caption: The Milky Way and laser guide stars above Gemini South, Cerro Pachón
story: The Milky Way flows across the southern night sky above Gemini South, which is sending up its five laser guide stars. A large red patch in the Milky Way at the centre of the frame is the Carina Nebula, which ranks among the biggest diffuse nebulae visible in our skies. To the left of the telescope, below the Milky Way, lie the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds.

Gemini South is one half of the International Gemini Observatory, which NSF NOIRLab operates with partial support from the U.S. National Science Foundation. It stands atop Cerro Pachón in Chile, a place known for its dark skies. Its advanced adaptive optics system uses the laser guide stars to reduce the blurring caused by Earth's atmosphere.

Constellations dotted through the Milky Way include Centaurus, Crux and Canis Major, which holds Sirius, the brightest star in the sky. The Magellanic Clouds are dwarf galaxies that orbit our own, making them our nearest galactic neighbours, and their closeness lets astronomers study their stars in detail.
explore: Indigenous cultures of the southern hemisphere have known the Magellanic Clouds for thousands of years, and they also appear in accounts by early explorers from the northern hemisphere. The photograph was taken during the NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition by Petr Horálek, a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador.

understand.summary: A night-sky landscape photograph by Petr Horálek. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the night sky would look fainter to someone standing at the site.

alt: The Milky Way flowing across the sky above the Gemini South telescope as it projects laser beams, with a large red nebula at centre and the Magellanic Clouds to the left.

caption: Gemini South and Rubin Observatory under the Milky Way, Cerro Pachón
story: Over Cerro Pachón in the Chilean Andes, the Milky Way appears to float just above the horizon, and the streak of light left by a meteor appears to slice straight through it. Against the starry sky stands the silhouette of Gemini South, the southern member of NSF NOIRLab's International Gemini Observatory.

Each of the twin Gemini telescopes, this one and Gemini North, is 8.1 meters in diameter. The pair occupy two of the finest observing sites on Earth, with Gemini North on the peak of Maunakea, a dormant Hawaiian volcano.

The picture also catches the outline of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which was under construction on Cerro Pachón at the time. Beside its unfinished dome, the tiny shape of a construction crane is just visible. Once finished, Rubin was to use its 8-meter telescope and 3.2-gigapixel camera for a decade-long survey that would cover the entire visible southern sky every few nights.
explore: The credit names the photographer as Kwon O Chul. The photograph shows the two observatories side by side on the same mountain, one working and one still being built.

understand.summary: A night-sky landscape photograph by Kwon O Chul. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the night sky would look fainter to someone standing at the site.

alt: The Milky Way above the silhouettes of Gemini South and the unfinished Rubin Observatory dome, crossed by the streak of a meteor.

caption: A lunar eclipse near moonrise, Gemini North
story: Far off on the right side of this photograph, a lunar eclipse sits within a dark blue band above the horizon, as seen from Gemini North. The telescope is one half of the International Gemini Observatory, which NSF NOIRLab operates with partial support from the U.S. National Science Foundation. The picture was captured in 2019.
A lunar eclipse happens when Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon. The Moon shines only by reflected sunlight, so when it moves into Earth's shadow it darkens.

Anyone on the side of Earth where the Moon is up can watch such an eclipse. How much of the Moon is covered depends on how closely it lines up with Earth's shadow and on where the observer stands. In 2022, for example, both lunar eclipses were total, and both could be seen from Gemini North in Hawai‘i. Events like these are an endless source of excitement for the observatory's staff.

understand.summary: A landscape photograph by J. Chu. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: The eclipse itself is visible to the naked eye, but no camera details are published, so it is unclear how closely the photograph matches what an eye would see.

alt: A distant lunar eclipse on the right, sitting in a dark blue band above the horizon, seen from Gemini North.

caption: Star trails above the SOAR Telescope, Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory
story: Shortly before sunrise, stars appear to trail in circles above the Southern Astrophysical Research (SOAR) Telescope. At the centre of the circles lies the south celestial pole. A few airplanes, shooting stars and satellites have left faint trails as well. SOAR belongs to NSF NOIRLab's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory.

The trails come from the rotation of Earth. Over a long exposure, the turning planet makes each star smear into an arc across the frame, and the arcs grow longer the longer the camera keeps collecting light.

Research telescopes cannot accept that smearing. To produce sharp images of stars, planets and galaxies, instruments like SOAR rely on sophisticated tracking and guiding systems that follow their targets precisely, sometimes for hours at a time. Combined with adaptive optics, which correct for the blurring caused by the atmosphere, these systems let modern telescopes make clear images of every type of celestial object.
explore: The credit names the photographer as M. Paredes. NOIRLab released the picture as an Image of the Week under the title "Star Trails over SOAR".

understand.summary: A long-exposure night photograph by M. Paredes. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points, and the trails appear only because the camera kept recording while Earth turned.

alt: Circular star trails around the south celestial pole above the SOAR Telescope, with a few faint trails from airplanes, meteors and satellites.

caption: Star trails above Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Cerro Pachón
story: Stars sweep across the southern sky above the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory, perched on Cerro Pachón, in this long exposure. That motion is only apparent, produced as Earth rotates. Rubin itself is built to capture real change in the Universe on a far larger scale.

When this photograph was released, the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) was still ahead. Over its 10 years, Rubin's data processing was expected to produce around 500 petabytes, more than all the text humans have ever written, in every language. The plan was for Rubin to scan the sky nightly with its LSST Camera.

By returning to the same sky again and again, Rubin was expected to flag millions of changes across the south every night, among them supernovae and pulsating variable stars. Its software compares each new image with earlier ones and picks out differences in near-real time. That gives scientists a better chance of finding and studying rare, short-lived events throughout the Universe.
explore: Funding for Rubin comes jointly from the U.S. National Science Foundation and the Office of Science within the U.S. Department of Energy. The photographer, Petr Horálek, is a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador, and NOIRLab released the picture as an Image of the Week.

understand.summary: A long-exposure night photograph by Petr Horálek. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points, and the trails appear only because the camera kept recording while Earth turned.

alt: Star trails sweeping across the southern sky above the Rubin Observatory on Cerro Pachón.

caption: Winter on Maunakea, home of Gemini North
story: Hawai‘i is known for tropical weather and volcanoes, but high up, winter storms can bring snow. NOIRLab titled this photograph "Hawaiian Snow". It comes from Maunakea, the mountain that hosts NSF NOIRLab's Gemini North telescope, one of the telescopes of the International Gemini Observatory.

Maunakea is one of five volcanoes that make up the island of Hawai‘i, and its summit stands at 4200 meters, about 14,000 feet. Winter snow is common enough up there, but luckily for Gemini North and its neighbouring telescopes, the mountain sees snowfall only a few times in a season.
For the rest of the year the summit is often above the clouds. Astronomers working there regularly look down and see nothing but a spread of cloud beneath them.
explore: The credit names the photographer as J. Chu. Gemini North shares the summit with other telescopes, and all of them benefit from snow being rare. NOIRLab released the photograph as an Image of the Week.

understand.summary: A landscape photograph of Maunakea by J. Chu. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: No camera details are published, so it is unclear how closely the photograph matches what an eye would see.

alt: A photograph titled Hawaiian Snow, taken on Maunakea, home of the Gemini North telescope.

caption: Moonset over Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Cerro Pachón
story: The Moon sets in a bright sky over the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory on Cerro Pachón in Chile. We tend to link the Moon with night, but it is visible in daylight nearly half the time.

Rubin will not observe the Moon, one of the most familiar sights in the sky. It is far too bright for Rubin's highly sensitive camera, which is designed to pick up much fainter light from distant galaxies or from nearer but dimmer objects such as asteroids and comets. The best nights for its deep-sky work come around new Moon, when the Moon is invisible and the sky is at its darkest. When the Moon is up, Rubin switches to a filter better suited to the brighter conditions and keeps collecting high-quality data.

The observatory takes its name from the astronomer Vera Rubin, whose work gave the first convincing evidence that dark matter exists. Using the largest camera ever built, it is designed to scan the sky repeatedly for 10 years and build an ultra-wide, ultra-high-definition time-lapse record of the Universe.
explore: Funding for Rubin comes jointly from the U.S. National Science Foundation and the Office of Science within the U.S. Department of Energy, and it is run jointly by NSF NOIRLab and DOE's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. The photographer, Petr Horálek, is a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador.

understand.summary: A landscape photograph by Petr Horálek. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: No camera details are published, so it is unclear how closely the photograph matches what an eye would see.

alt: The Moon setting in a bright sky over the Rubin Observatory on Cerro Pachón.

caption: Gemini North and neighbouring telescopes, Maunakea
story: Gemini North, second from the left, stands with five other telescopes near the summit of Maunakea in Hawai‘i in this timelapse image. Gemini North belongs to the International Gemini Observatory, operated by NSF NOIRLab.

Maunakea is one of the five volcanoes that form the island of Hawai‘i. Its summit, 4.2 kilometers (2.6 miles) high, sits above most of the island's tropical clouds and humidity. The environment up there is unlike the rest of the island. It can turn snowy from time to time, little rain falls, and the soil cannot support most plants. Low oxygen levels make it somewhat hazardous to stay for long.

Those harsh conditions are what make the summit good for astronomy. Above the thickest part of Earth's atmosphere, telescopes get sharper views and escape much of the turbulence that blurs distant stars and galaxies. The location also cuts down light scattered from light pollution and from natural effects in the atmosphere.
explore: The credit names the photographer as J. Chu. NOIRLab released the picture as an Image of the Week under the title "Silent Night, Starry Night". A timelapse like this combines many exposures into a single picture.

understand.summary: A timelapse night photograph by J. Chu. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: A timelapse combines many exposures, so it records more light and motion than the eye takes in at a single glance.

alt: Six telescopes near the summit of Maunakea under a night sky, with Gemini North second from the left.

caption: Sunset over Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory
story: Beneath an orange sky, the mountains of northern Chile recede into the distance in this sunset photograph of NSF NOIRLab's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO). Many of the observatory's telescopes jut from the mountain in the foreground. On the peak, the SMARTS Telescopes and the Víctor M. Blanco 4-m Telescope stand out, and smaller telescopes are spread along the ridge.
CTIO is home to more than 20 working telescopes, and a good number of them appear in the frame.

The scene looks calm, but the hours before dusk are busy ones for the engineers and astronomers at the observatory. They spend that time getting ready for a packed schedule of scientific observations. Observatories are usually built on high mountains like this one because the air above them is thinner, drier and steadier than the air lower down, which keeps images sharper.
explore: The credit names the photographer as B. Tafreshi. NOIRLab released the picture as an Image of the Week under the title "Sunset Skies at CTIO".

understand.summary: A sunset landscape photograph by B. Tafreshi. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: Sunset colours are visible to the naked eye, though camera settings can change how strong they look in a photograph.
